body_markdown:
The concept of a rear-mid-engine Corvette can be contentious in some automotive circles. Some folks love the rearward engine placement, and indeed, the C8 Corvette has an impressive level of performance and poise.[Even Zora wanted the switch](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/chevrolet-took-52-years-to-put-make-the-corvette-mid-engine/) . However, others contend that the C8 Corvette’s departure from a front-engine architecture is akin to betrayal. Both sides have valid points, because vehicles with decades of consistent performance history become legends, and even icons: Switching engine locations ensures the Corvette’s cab-backward, historically front-engine design turns into something cab-forward and distinctly exotic.


I tend to see things through a polarizing filter, but I wondered if my co-workers at Hagerty Media felt as strongly as I did, one way or another. So I posed the question, and braced myself for their reaction: *Is the Corvette better off as a mid-engine sports car?*


## Yes!


Chevrolet


“From a marketing and brand perspective, a mid-engine, high-performance, marquee sports car from GM just had to have the Corvette nameplate. No other way around it.” — *Ben Woodworth*


“Mid-engine for me! Early on, the Corvette managed to innovate regularly and offer things only available at much more exotic price points. Once it matured, even though Chevy continued to push the envelope, there arose a stalwart group of folks who had strong ideas on what a Corvette ‘should’ be. I don’t suspect that Zora would’ve been a part of that crowd.


“Although I greatly prefer the look and proportions of the C7 to those of the C8, it was time for the car to evolve so it could continue to succeed at offering super- and, now, hypercar performance at a still kinda-sorta achievable price.” — *Eddy Eckart*


“Remember that Zora wanted it mid-engine from the start—but I agree with Eddy on all points above and can’t really add much more. I’ve driven every generation Corvette. Those C5 through C7 cars were just…fast fun, the epitome of what a high-torque, high-horsepower, rear-drive sports car should be. The roar off the line, the back end sliding around corners, and the iconic styling … They just got better with each new iteration, and their racing record proves it.


“The C8 is a magnificent machine, nimble and modern, but more in line with a McLaren or Ferrari. It lost a little bit of its American soul when the engine moved. And I’m personally not a fan of that exterior design.” — *Todd Kraemer*


“The Corvette is complicated. I admire the engineering brilliance that the Corvette team applied to the C8, creating incredible performance for a fraction of the price of European supercar rivals. But the car is singularly unattractive, so it doesn’t really matter how much power it has or how well it drives.


“The last part of the equation is for the Corvette design team to make a[beautiful C9](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/c9-corvette-pondering-the-next-generation-of-an-american-legend/) . All that said, it’s unfortunate that while the Corvette chases Lamborghinis, Ferraris, and McLarens, GM abandons those who might enjoy an affordable RWD car. Like a Camaro!” — *Joe DeMatio*


“To Joe’s point, America is in a horsepower war and losing to imported brands is not an option. Lamborghinis aren’t rare anymore, nor are Ferraris or McLarens. The insane levels of horsepower present on city streets and interstate highways mean the Corvette must adapt if it wants to keep its crown of performance with impressive value.


“The beauty of General Motors since the early days is that it had the manufacturing might to trample the competition, be that meant snatching away market share from Ford with the ’27 Chevrolet AA, or changing the trajectory of GM’s motorsports efforts with the C5-R’s impressive victories. That Corvette Racing team[likely influenced](https://www.imsahalloffame.com/drivers/corvette-c5-r/#:~:text=The%20key%20to,has%20been%20accomplished.) our current C8 Corvette, so the mid-engine move is a self-inflicted change. I hope the next (C9) Corvette will have less try-hard styling, but I look forward to racing versions of the ZR1 and ZR1-X absolutely trampling on their competition. You know, the way GM has always done it.” — *Sajeev Mehta*


## No!


GM


“The Corvette is the following: Front-engine, V-8-powered, rear-wheel-drive, two-door (coupe, targa, convertible), and preferably with a manual option. When the engine is behind the driver in a GM-based product, it can be called a Fiero or a Corvair—take your pick.


“That being said, C8 ZR1X is *nutso butso* , and I’d take one if given to me … and then rebadge it as a Corvair!” — *Matt Tuccillo*


“It’s funny: I had some pretty good contacts at Chevrolet and knew well what they were doing to the C8 Corvette—and one reason for that was the fact that the front-engine car could no longer compete in a field full of mid- or rear-engine cars in IMSA and in the WEC. The transition made perfect sense, and mechanically, it’s a home run. So why am I so attracted to the C6, and especially the C7?


“I was there when GM rolled out the C8, in the old blimp hangar in Tustin, California, and seeing it in the flesh—I dunno, it was kind of like watching a sequel made to a favorite movie that left you a little wanting (imagine *Forrest Gump 2* ). On paper, the C8 ticked every box, and it’s a wonderful car to drive, and that first year, you could get a helluva deal on one. But I wish they’d edited in a little more Corvette-ness, starting with round taillights. I can’t really fault it, but I don’t love it like I expected to.” — *Steven Cole Smith*


“I was also in that hangar in Tustin, and didn’t know Steven was there. I was very impressed by the value at the time, and I do enjoy the design, especially the widebody variants. It’s clearly a much better performance car; I can accept that. It has also sold well and probably changed the buying demographic in huge ways, and both of those things are big wins for the brand. That said, I don’t have much desire to own a C8.


“I would gladly make room in my garage for a C3 or a C7, but I know that I’m not a great performance driver, and wouldn’t need to get the absolute most out of it on the track. In that way, I guess I would be the stereotypical Corvette owner.


“Not that anyone asked, but I thought that the Corvette going mid-engine would have been a sign that Camaro had lots of room to grow and not step on any toes. Oh well.” — *Brandan Gillogly*


The post[Our Two Cents: Mid-Engine Corvette or No?](https://www.hagerty.com/media/hagerty-community/our-two-cents-mid-engine-corvette-or-no/) appeared first on[Hagerty Media](https://www.hagerty.com/media) .
